slides.title: What Is the Point of Hyperbolic Functions?

shapes.alt: The chain segment from C to R has leftward tension at C, tangent tension at R and downward weight through its centre of mass.
A uniform metal chain hanging freely between two level supports.

transcription.tex: Hyperbolic functions arise when we solve differential equations in mechanics. A uniform hanging chain provides an example.\par Consider the blue segment from its lowest point $C$ to a point $R$. Its arc length is $s$. If the mass per unit length is $\lambda$, its mass is $\lambda s$.\par Three forces keep this segment in equilibrium. At $C$ the tension $T_0$ acts horizontally. At $R$ the tension $T$ acts along the tangent. The weight $\lambda g s$ acts vertically downwards, where $g$ is gravitational acceleration.

The equilibrium equations give a catenary. With $c=T_0/(\lambda g)$ and the lowest point at $(0,c)$, its equation is $y=c\cosh(x/c)$.\par Measuring both coordinates in units of $c$ gives the normalised equation $y=\cosh x$.

transcription.tex: Why is there a problem finding the inverse of \(f(x)=\cosh x\)?\par A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one. transcription.tex: Hyperbolic functions are exponential, so their inverses can be expressed using logarithms.\par Prove \(\operatorname{arsinh}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1})\).
\[e^y=\frac{2x\pm\sqrt{4x^2+4}}2=x\pm\sqrt{x^2+1}.\]Since \(\sqrt{x^2+1}>|x|\) and \(e^y>0\), only the positive sign is possible.

transcription.tex: \[y=\operatorname{arcosh}x\Rightarrow x=\cosh y=\frac{e^y+e^{-y}}2\]\[e^y+e^{-y}=2x\Rightarrow e^{2y}-2xe^y+1=0.\]\[a=1,\ b=-2x,\ c=1\]\[e^y=\frac{2x\pm\sqrt{4x^2-4}}2=x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}.\]Both roots are positive, but the principal inverse has \(y\ge0\). Thus\[y=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}).\]
Show why the other logarithm is non-positive.
\[(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})=1\]\[x-\sqrt{x^2-1}=\frac1{x+\sqrt{x^2-1}}\]\[\ln(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})=-\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})\le0.\]Equality occurs only at \(x=1\), where both branches give zero.

transcription.tex: (a) Show that \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(arsinh x\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\) [We did this earlier]\par (b) Find the first two non-zero terms of the series expansion of \(arsinh x\).\par The general form for the series expansion of \(arsinh x\) is given by\par \(arsinh x=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty } \left(\frac{{\left(-1\right)}^{n}\left(2n\right)!}{{2}^{2n}{\left(n!\right)}^{2}}\right)\frac{{x}^{2n+1}}{2n+1}\)\par (c) Find, in simplest terms, the coefficient of \({x}^{5}\).\par (d) Use your approximation up to and including the term in \({x}^{5}\) to find an approximate value for \(arsinh 0.5\).\par (e) Calculate the percentage error in using this approximation.

\[f(x)=\operatorname{arsinh}x,\quad f(0)=0\]\[f^{\prime}(x)=(1+x^2)^{-1/2},\quad f^{\prime}(0)=1\]\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=-x(1+x^2)^{-3/2},\quad f^{\prime\prime}(0)=0\]\[f^{\prime\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{2x^2-1}{(1+x^2)^{5/2}},\quad f^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)=-1.\]Continue until two non-zero terms appear:\[f(x)=f(0)+f^{\prime}(0)x+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2+\frac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)}{3!}x^3+\cdots\]\[\operatorname{arsinh}x\approx x-\frac{x^3}{6}.\]

transcription.tex: Find \(\int\cosh^5(2x)\sinh(2x)\,dx\).\par Recall the “consider and scale” method used for \(\int\sin^n x\cos x\,dx\) and \(\int\cos^n x\sin x\,dx\).
Find \(\int\tanh x\,dx\).\par As for ordinary tan, first express the function as a quotient.
\[\int\tanh x\,dx=\int\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}\,dx\]\[=\ln|\cosh x|+C.\]There is no minus sign: cosh differentiates to positive sinh. Also \(\cosh x>0\), so the modulus can be omitted.

transcription.tex: For \(a>0\), choose sensible substitutions.\par Recall \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\), and \(1+\sinh^2u=\cosh^2u\).

Use \(x=a\sinh u\). The denominator becomes \(a\cosh u\) and \(dx=a\cosh u\,du\), so they cancel.\par With \(x=a\tan\theta\), the denominator gives \(a\sec\theta\) but \(dx=a\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\), leaving an extra sec factor.

transcription.tex: Show \(\int\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}x+\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+C\).\par Hint: use a sensible substitution. Recall \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\), \(1+\sinh^2u=\cosh^2u\).

Try \(x=\tan\theta\), \(-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2\):\[dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta,\quad I=\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta.\]Integrate by parts with \(u=\sec\theta\), \(dv/d\theta=\sec^2\theta\), hence \(du/d\theta=\sec\theta\tan\theta\), \(v=\tan\theta\):\[I=\sec\theta\tan\theta-\int\sec\theta\tan^2\theta\,d\theta\]\[=\sec\theta\tan\theta-\int\sec\theta(\sec^2\theta-1)\,d\theta\]\[=\sec\theta\tan\theta-I+\int\sec\theta\,d\theta.\]\[2I=\sec\theta\tan\theta+\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C\]\[I=\tfrac12\sec\theta\tan\theta+\tfrac12\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C\]\[=\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\tfrac12\ln|\sqrt{1+x^2}+x|+C\]\[=\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}x+C.\]

Try \(x=\sinh u\):\[dx=\cosh u\,du\]\[I=\int\cosh u\cosh u\,du=\int\cosh^2u\,du\]\[=\tfrac12\int(1+\cosh2u)\,du\]\[=\tfrac12\left(u+\tfrac12\sinh2u\right)+C\]\[=\tfrac12u+\tfrac12\sinh u\cosh u+C\]\[=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}x+\tfrac12x\sqrt{1+x^2}+C.\]This substitution gives the shorter method.

transcription.tex: Use the substitution $x=\sinh^2u$ to find $\int\sqrt{\frac{x}{x+1}}\,\mathrm dx$, $x>0$.

\(x=\sinh^2u,\quad u>0,\quad \mathrm dx=2\sinh u\cosh u\,\mathrm du,\quad \frac{x}{x+1}=\frac{\sinh^2u}{1+\sinh^2u}=\frac{\sinh^2u}{\cosh^2u}\)\par \(\int\sqrt{\frac{x}{x+1}}\,\mathrm dx=\int\frac{\sinh u}{\cosh u}\cdot2\sinh u\cosh u\,\mathrm du=\int2\sinh^2u\,\mathrm du\)\par \(=\int(\cosh2u-1)\,\mathrm du=\tfrac12\sinh2u-u+C\)\par \(=\sinh u\cosh u-\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt x+C\)\par \(=\sqrt x\sqrt{1+x}-\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt x+C\)

transcription.tex: By using the substitution $u=x^2$, evaluate $\int_2^3\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^4-1}}\,\mathrm dx$.

\(u=x^2,\quad\mathrm du=2x\,\mathrm dx;\quad x=2\Rightarrow u=4,\quad x=3\Rightarrow u=9\)\par \(\int_2^3\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^4-1}}\,\mathrm dx=\int_4^9\frac{\mathrm du}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\)\par \(=\bigl[\operatorname{arcosh}u\bigr]_4^9=\operatorname{arcosh}9-\operatorname{arcosh}4\)\par \(=0.824\quad(3\ \text{s.f.})\)

transcription.tex: Use the substitution $x=2\cosh u$ to show that\par $\int\sqrt{x^2-4}\,\mathrm dx=\frac12x\sqrt{x^2-4}-2\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+c$

\(x=2\cosh u,\quad u\ge0,\quad\mathrm dx=2\sinh u\,\mathrm du\)\par \(I=\int\sqrt{x^2-4}\,\mathrm dx=\int2\sqrt{\cosh^2u-1}\cdot2\sinh u\,\mathrm du=4\int\sinh^2u\,\mathrm du\)\par \(=2\int(\cosh2u-1)\,\mathrm du=2\left(\tfrac12\sinh2u-u\right)+c=2\sinh u\cosh u-2u+c\)\par \(\cosh u=\tfrac x2,\quad\sinh u=\sqrt{(x/2)^2-1}=\tfrac12\sqrt{x^2-4},\quad u=\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\tfrac x2\right)\)\par \(I=2\left(\tfrac12\sqrt{x^2-4}\right)\left(\tfrac x2\right)-2\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\tfrac x2\right)+c\)\par \(=\tfrac12x\sqrt{x^2-4}-2\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\tfrac x2\right)+c\)

transcription.tex: (a) Show that $\int\frac{1}{2\cosh x-\sinh x}\,\mathrm dx$ can be written as $\int\frac{2e^x}{e^{2x}+3}\,\mathrm dx$.\par (b) Hence, by using the substitution $u=e^x$, find $\int\frac{1}{2\cosh x-\sinh x}\,\mathrm dx$.

(a) \(2\cosh x-\sinh x=2\left(\frac{e^x+e^{-x}}2\right)-\left(\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}2\right)\)\par \(=\frac{e^x+3e^{-x}}2\)\par \(\int\frac1{2\cosh x-\sinh x}\,\mathrm dx=\int\frac2{e^x+3e^{-x}}\,\mathrm dx\)\par \(=\int\frac{2e^x}{e^{2x}+3}\,\mathrm dx\)

transcription.tex: Using the substitution $u=\frac23\sinh x$, evaluate $\int_0^1\frac{\cosh x}{\sqrt{4\sinh^2x+9}}\,\mathrm dx$.

\(u=\tfrac23\sinh x,\quad \mathrm du=\tfrac23\cosh x\,\mathrm dx,\quad \cosh x\,\mathrm dx=\tfrac32\,\mathrm du\)\par \(4\sinh^2x+9=4\left(\tfrac{3u}{2}\right)^2+9=9(u^2+1)\)\par \(x=0\Rightarrow u=0,\quad x=1\Rightarrow u=\tfrac23\sinh1\)\par \(\int_0^1\frac{\cosh x}{\sqrt{4\sinh^2x+9}}\,\mathrm dx=\int_0^{(2/3)\sinh1}\frac1{3\sqrt{u^2+1}}\cdot\tfrac32\,\mathrm du\)\par \(=\left[\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}u\right]_0^{(2/3)\sinh1}=\tfrac12\operatorname{arsinh}\left(\tfrac23\sinh1\right)=0.360\quad(3\ \text{s.f.})\)

transcription.tex: \(3x^2-6x+7=3\left(x^2-2x+\tfrac73\right)=3\left((x-1)^2+\tfrac43\right)\)\par \(u=x-1,\quad \mathrm du=\mathrm dx;\quad x=1\Rightarrow u=0,\quad x=3\Rightarrow u=2\)\par \(\int_1^3\frac{\mathrm dx}{\sqrt{3x^2-6x+7}}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\int_0^2\frac{\mathrm du}{\sqrt{u^2+(2/\sqrt3)^2}}\)\par \(=\frac1{\sqrt3}\left[\operatorname{arsinh}\left(\frac{\sqrt3u}{2}\right)\right]_0^2=\frac1{\sqrt3}\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt3\)\par \(=\frac1{\sqrt3}\ln(\sqrt3+\sqrt{3+1})=\frac1{\sqrt3}\ln(2+\sqrt3)\)
